transcript.text: We want to reduce B2B SaaS subscription churn before annual renewal, but we do not have a clean dataset yet. We have 5,000 enterprise accounts, an 8% annual churn rate, a $50 CSM intervention cost, and $2,500 saved per retained account.

What the problem is  
The decision is whether a customer success team should take preventive action on selected enterprise accounts before their annual renewal, in order to keep them from churning. The result would be used by CSMs and renewal owners to decide which accounts to work on, and by leadership to judge whether intervention is worth doing. The unit is an enterprise account during a renewal cycle, and the moment is before the renewal outcome is locked in.

What is known  
You gave 5,000 enterprise accounts, an 8% annual churn rate, a $50 intervention cost, and $2,500 saved per retained account. That tells you the business scale and the basic cost-to-value relationship. It does not tell you which accounts are actually at risk, when risk should be acted on, whether a CSM touch prevents churn, or how much intervention capacity exists.

What is not known  
There is no clean dataset yet, so it is unclear whether you have reliable account identifiers, renewal dates, contract details, usage signals, support issues, executive sponsorship, renewal intent, prior outreach, or historical intervention outcomes. It is also unclear whether churn can be defined consistently as cancellation, non-renewal, downgraded renewal, or delayed renewal. CSM capacity and response rates are unknown too.

Approaches that could solve it  
A no-model operational approach could work: rank accounts using known business rules such as renewal date, weak executive sponsorship, declining product usage, support friction, contract complications, and strategic account importance. This is fast, cheap, transparent, and usable immediately, but it is limited to existing knowledge and cannot prove which accounts actually need intervention.

A simple statistical risk model could predict churn likelihood by renewal time using account, usage, contract, and support features. This gives better ranking and can uncover non-obvious risk patterns, but it needs clean labels, stable features, and careful validation. It predicts churn, not whether a CSM touch changes the outcome.

An intervention-focused approach would model or test which accounts respond to CSM effort rather than just which are risky. This may include experiments, matched controls, or uplift-style models. This is the most useful for business value, but it costs time and requires logging what was done, when, and whether the account renewed.

Chosen plan  
Start with a data-first, no-model risk list, then build a model only after the data and intervention tracking are reliable. That path is appropriate because you do not have a clean dataset yet, but you still have an actionable renewal window.

Begin by defining the label and the timing window. Decide what counts as churn for this program, for example no renewal or cancellation by the renewal decision point. Choose a fixed lead time before renewal when a CSM can realistically act. This timing must be decided with the business, not inferred from data alone.

Define the unit as account-renewal episode. One account may have multiple renewal cycles over time, so the future dataset should not treat each account as only one row unless you are explicitly modeling lifetime risk.

Inventory the data sources needed for that unit: billing, CRM, product usage, support tickets, account management notes, executive sponsorship, contract terms, renewal status, and CSM activity logs. Without these, any model will be guessing.

Create the minimum clean table first: account identifier, renewal date, churn outcome, intervention date if any, intervention owner, intervention type, and whether the intervention happened before the risk could be acted on. This table is more important than adding many advanced features too soon.

Build the initial no-model list using clear, explainable signals. Put highest priority on accounts that are both high risk and valuable, and on accounts where renewal is imminent enough for a CSM to act. If CSM capacity is unknown, start with a short reviewable list and adjust it as workload becomes visible.

Instrument every intervention. Record whether a CSM touched the account, what action was taken, when it happened, and what the renewal outcome was. If safe, hold back some comparable accounts for comparison. This is how you later learn whether the intervention actually saves accounts or whether you were just spending time on accounts that were likely to renew anyway.

Check the result by looking at untouched historical renewals and asking whether the high-risk list ranked churners better than low-risk accounts. Then check current operations by comparing intervened accounts with similar non-intervened accounts, if available. The goal is not perfect prediction; the goal is better prioritization and measurable retained value versus intervention cost.

When the data is clean enough and the label is stable, move to a simple risk model. Use it to rank accounts within the pre-renewal window and evaluate it against the no-model list on held-out renewal cycles. If the model adds little, keep the operational rules. If it adds clear lift, integrate it into CSM workflow.

Only later consider an intervention-effect model. That requires repeated, logged CSM actions and ideally randomized or well-matched comparisons. It is the right tool if the main question becomes “who can be saved by doing something,” not just “who is likely to churn.”

When to stop  
Stop building if you cannot reliably record renewal outcomes or intervention exposure, because then any model is unverifiable. Stop expanding complexity if the simple list already identifies the same accounts you can realistically serve. Stop a specific intervention type if controls or comparisons show it does not improve renewal. Stop optimizing for prediction if the business cannot act on the results in time before renewal.

transcript.text: I run operations for a furniture retailer with one warehouse. The owner wants to know whether we should open a second warehouse in the south next year. Nothing is in a system I could export for you: I have what I know from the job. Deliveries to the south take about 6 days, to the north 2. Around a third of our orders go south. How should we think about this?

The problem is not really “predict deliveries.” It is “decide whether adding a southern stock location creates enough value to pay for itself.” The owner needs the yes/no recommendation. You need it to decide the warehouse setup for the coming year. The unit of analysis is the order, grouped by region. The moment that matters is the commitment for the next year: where inventory will be placed before orders arrive.

What you have told me: deliveries to the south take about 6 days; deliveries to the north take about 2 days; around a third of orders go south; you currently operate from one warehouse.

What is not known and what matters: whether customers value shorter south delivery enough to win or save sales; whether the 6-day south wait causes complaints, lost sales, or extra cost; what the warehouse will cost in rent, labor, stock, transfers, and complexity; how inventory carrying cost changes when stock is duplicated; whether adding southern inventory worsens north service; whether outside providers, cross-docking, or partial southern stocking could give the benefit without a full warehouse; and whether south orders differ by item size, season, value, or service promise.

A useful framing is this: a new southern site is worth it if the value gained on southern orders — better service, less lost sales, lower delivery cost, happier customers, more sales — is greater than the added cost of having a second stock location, including duplicated inventory and the risk of lower north performance. Because only about a third of orders go south, the benefit per southern order must be strong enough to support the extra cost.

Approaches you could take:

- No model at all: decide by judgment. This is quick and cheap. It can be right if the service pain or cost burden is obvious. It gives no protection from being wrong about the trade-off.

- Manual descriptive review: go through invoices, carrier records, complaints, stockout notes, or paper logs to see the share of south orders, lead time variability, and visible service problems. This costs some time but helps locate the real pain. It does not yet say whether a warehouse is economically justified.

- Simple scenario spreadsheet: build a small cost-and-service trade-off comparing the current setup, a southern warehouse, and any interim alternatives. This is the most useful approach right now. It needs estimated ranges, not perfect data. It gives a clear view of what would have to be true for the decision to change.

- Inventory or fulfillment simulation/optimization: model stock placement, lead times, demand, and service levels. This is powerful but expensive. It requires detailed order, inventory, cost, and timing data. It is premature given what you have now.

I would choose the simple scenario spreadsheet, plus a small reversible pilot if needed. Do not start with machine learning. There is not enough data, and the core issue is economic trade-off, not prediction.

Plan:

Begin by writing the decision clearly: “Should we open a southern warehouse for the next year, or can we achieve the needed service benefit another way?” Define the owner’s goal as protecting or improving value: revenue, margin, customer satisfaction, and operational control.

Then list the options. Compare the current warehouse arrangement. Compare a new southern warehouse. Compare interim choices such as using an external southern provider, sending stock to a local point only for best-moving items, negotiating faster south delivery, or accepting the current south lead time. Each option should be described by lead time, cost, service effect, risk, and flexibility.

Gather the minimum facts you can get by hand. Do not demand perfect data. Use:

- approximate order volume by region and by item type, even in broad bands;
- current delivery cost patterns, especially anything specific to the south;
- whether south orders have different value, size, season, or service expectations;
- evidence of lost sales, complaints, or reorders caused by the south lead time;
- what a southern warehouse would cost in rent, fit-out, labor, stock, transfers, returns, and management attention;
- how inventory carrying cost changes if stock is duplicated;
- the risk that keeping less inventory in the main warehouse slows north orders;
- whether an outside provider could give part of the benefit without a full warehouse.

Build a simple spreadsheet. For each option, estimate the value gained and the cost added. You do not need a prediction model. You need a range: what happens if the service benefit is weak, and what happens if it is strong; what happens if costs are high, and what happens if they are low. This gives a “bad case / good case” view.

The key calculation is conceptually: value gained from faster or better southern fulfillment must exceed the added cost and risk of duplicating stock and operating another location. If the decision flips depending on which assumption you make, write down the assumption that controls the result. That tells you what to investigate next.

Then choose a check. If the spreadsheet says “yes, even in the bad case,” it may be enough to proceed, subject to finance and capacity review. If it says “no, even in the good case,” reject it for now. If it says “maybe,” do not open a permanent warehouse yet. Run a small, reversible test instead: use a southern third-party storage or fulfillment point, pre-position only key items, or use cross-docking for a short period. Measure south delivery times, complaints, stockout issues, extra costs, and any change in sales or service quality.

The result is checked in layers. First, sanity-check the assumption that a southern site actually shortens south lead time. Second, check whether it harms north lead time or increases stockout risk. Third, compare the pilot or assumed service improvement with the extra cost and operational burden. Fourth, ask whether the decision survives when you make the cost estimate less favorable and the service benefit estimate less favorable. If it does, the case is stronger. If it does not, you need better information before committing capital.

Stop and decide when the answer is stable across plausible assumptions. If one unknown controls everything, stop only when that unknown has been measured or tested. If the owner is willing to accept the risk anyway, that becomes the business decision, not the data decision.

The short version: think of this as a service-versus-cost trade-off. A southern warehouse is justified only if the benefit it brings to the portion of orders going south is enough to cover the added warehouse and inventory cost, without hurting the north. With only the facts you gave, the answer cannot be known yet. Use a simple scenario spreadsheet, then a small pilot if the spreadsheet leaves the result unresolved.
